# Genesis 35: verse-by-verse research notes

**What I could and couldn't cover:** I ran out of searches before I could read pages from the Catholic or Orthodox sites (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org), bibleodyssey, netbible or most of the denominational sites. The Catholic and modern-scholarship points below come from older commentaries reprinted on studylight.org and biblehub.com. The pages I read don't show a real Protestant split on this chapter, so section 2 only notes small differences of emphasis. I found almost nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching; the one item is under v. 16.

## 1. Verse by verse

**v. 1:** Guzik says the trouble at Shechem in chapter 34 happened because Jacob went to Shechem instead of Bethel, where God had apparently called him to go (Genesis 31:13). He also notes that chapter 34 never mentions God, while chapter 35 names him more than ten times. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-35/
- Keil and Delitzsch: Jacob had allowed ten years to pass since his return from Mesopotamia, without performing the vow which he made at Bethel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/35-1.htm
- Constable thinks the delay evidently was due in part to the continuing presence of the idols that Rachel and probably others had brought from Haran. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/35-2.html
- Utley says "go up" may simply mean Bethel is higher ground, or it may be the verb used for going up to a holy place. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/genesis-35.html

**v. 2:** Commentators disagree about what the "foreign gods" were.
- Barnes says they include the teraphim, which Rachel had secreted, and the rings which were worn as amulets or charms. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/35-2.html
- Gill doubts that Laban's idols would have been kept so many years. He thinks they belonged to newly acquired Canaanite servants or captives, or came with the plunder of Shechem. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/35-2.html
- Clarke points out that Jacob's servants were Syrians and probably given to idolatry. Calvin says that by calling them "strange gods," Jacob convicts and condemns both himself and the rest. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/35-2.html
- On the washing and the change of clothes, Utley says the outward act shows the spiritual preparation necessary for renewing the covenant promises, and compares it to the covenant renewal in Joshua 24. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/genesis-35.html
- Guzik applies the verse to fathers: Jacob's family got right with God only after he did. He quotes Barnhouse that garments in the Bible stand for character. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-35/

**v. 3:** Utley wonders whether Jacob was by this point a full monotheist or still a "henotheist," worshipping one God for his own family without denying others. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-35

**v. 4:**
- The earrings: Utley says they apparently were magical charms tied to idolatry. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-35
- Guzik quotes Spurgeon guessing that they were charms. He applies the verse by urging readers to remove anything occult from their homes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-35/
- The tree: Keil thinks it was probably the very tree under which Abraham once pitched his tent (Genesis 12:6). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/35-7.htm
- Utley says the Hebrew word is "terebinth," and that the verb can mean "hide" or "bury." He reads the act as a clean break with the household's past religion. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-35

**v. 5:**
- Keil calls this a supernatural terror. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/35-7.htm
- Matthew Henry: while there was sin in Jacob's house he feared his neighbours, but once the idols were gone, his neighbours feared him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/35-2.html
- Utley sees "holy war" language here. He adds that the phrase could simply mean "a great terror." https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-35
- Guzik: God would have been fair to leave Jacob to the results of Shechem, but grace covered him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-35/

**v. 6:** Utley explains that "Luz" means "almond tree" and was the Canaanite name for the town. "Bethel," meaning "house of God," was the name Jacob gave the place nearby. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-35

**v. 7:**
- The Pulpit Commentary says building the altar was Jacob thus redeeming his vow. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/35-7.htm
- Matthew Henry's comment on the name El-bethel ("God of Bethel"): believers' comfort comes not so much from Beth-el, the house of God, as from El-beth-el, the God of the house. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/35-7.htm
- Benson guesses that Jacob also offered the tithe he had vowed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/35-7.htm
- Utley notes that the verb "revealed Himself" is plural in Hebrew, which is unusual. He suggests a link to the angels in Genesis 28. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-35

**v. 8:**
- Allon-bachuth means "Oak of Weeping." Guzik says nothing is known of Deborah before this, and we can't be sure how she came to be in Jacob's household. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-35/
- Barnes thinks Rebekah had probably already died, which would explain why her nurse was with Jacob. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/35-21.html
- Utley takes this small detail as a sign of an eyewitness source. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-35

**v. 9:** Guzik says God appearing "again" shows that Jacob's relationship with God had been restored. He maps the return to Bethel onto Revelation 2:4–5: remember, repent, and do the first works. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-35/

**v. 10:**
- Guzik: Jacob had been living like the old Jacob, so God reminds him of his new name. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-35/
- Barnes says the renaming shows that Jacob's spiritual life had declined between Penuel and Bethel and was now revived. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/35-11.htm
- Utley says the meaning of the name "Israel" is uncertain, and that this meeting may look back to 32:28. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-35

**v. 11:**
- "God Almighty" is El Shaddai, the name God used when he made his covenant with Abraham (Ellicott). https://biblehub.com/genesis/35-11.htm
- Calvin: God proclaims his own might, in order that Jacob may the more certainly rely on his faithfulness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/35-11.html
- "Kings": Calvin applies this properly to David's line, not to Saul or the northern kingdom. Gill includes Saul, David and Solomon, and especially the King Messiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/35-11.html
- Barnes: Abraham and Isaac had each only one son of promise. But now the time of increase is come. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/35-11.htm

**v. 12:** Wesley says the promises of the seed and the land had a spiritual meaning: Christ is the promised seed, and heaven is the promised land. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/genesis-35.html

**v. 13:** Guzik thinks God may have appeared here in bodily form. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-35/ Utley says the repeated phrase "where He had spoken with him" may be a copying slip (writing the same words twice). https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-35

**v. 14:** Utley notes that the drink offering and the oil use two different verbs. The oil is the kind used for holy anointings. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-35 Guzik connects the drink offering to Paul's picture of his life being poured out (Philippians 2:17). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-35/

**v. 15:** The naming of Bethel is recorded three times. Utley compares this to Acts telling Paul's conversion three times, and rejects the view that it shows different authors. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-35

**v. 16:** Keil says leaving Bethel did not break the command to "settle there." The word didn't require a permanent home, only that Jacob stay long enough to keep his vow. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/35-19.htm

**v. 17:** Utley says the midwife's words seem to fulfil Rachel's prayer in Genesis 30:24 for another son. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/genesis-35.html Matthew Henry: Rachel had passionately said, Give me children, or else I die; and now that she had children, she died! https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/35-19.htm

**v. 18:**
- Ben-oni means "son of my sorrow"; Benjamin means "son of my right hand." Guzik sees the end of the sisters' rivalry: Rachel's final "win" brought only sorrow. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-35/
- Utley says Mari texts suggest the name could also mean "son of the south." He also cautions against reading Greek ideas of the soul into "her soul was departing." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/genesis-35.html

**v. 19:**
- Gill links this to Matthew 2, where Rachel is pictured weeping for Bethlehem's children killed by Herod. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/35-19.htm
- For a different view, see "Modern scholarship" in section 3.

**v. 20:**
- Keil says "to this day" could have been written just ten or twenty years after the event. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/35-19.htm
- Matthew Henry notes the place later fell within Benjamin's land (1 Samuel 10:2). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/35-19.html

**v. 21:**
- Constable says the "tower of Eder" was a shepherds' watchtower. He adds that since Jerome it has been placed close to Bethlehem. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/35-19.html
- Clarke cites the Targum of Jonathan, which calls it the place where the King Messiah will be revealed. Gill suggests it was where the shepherds heard the angels in Luke 2. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/35-21.html

**v. 22:**
- Poole calls this a horrid incest; for concubines were a sort of wives. Wesley says this sin is why Reuben lost his birthright. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/35-22.htm
- The BibleHub study notes describe the act as a challenge to Jacob's authority over the household. Jacob deals with it later, in Genesis 49:3–4. https://biblehub.com/genesis/35-22.htm
- Ligonier suggests Reuben, as Leah's son, wanted to keep Rachel's maid from becoming Jacob's new favourite. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/one-sin-twelve-sons
- Clarke reports the Targum's softer reading, that Reuben only overturned Bilhah's bed. He says he would welcome it if it could be proved. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/35-22.html

**vv. 23–26:**
- "Born in Paddan-aram" includes Benjamin, who was born in Canaan. Benson explains this as a figure of speech that describes the whole group by what is true of most of it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/35-22.htm
- Coffman notes that the list orders the sons by mother. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/35-22.html

**v. 27:** Keil: arriving at Mamre meant Jacob was entering his father's house as Isaac's heir. He had probably visited before, but those visits didn't matter to the story. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/35-29.htm

**v. 28:**
- Barnes reckons Isaac was about 163 when Jacob returned. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/35-29.htm
- Constable says Isaac lived about 12 more years after Jacob moved to Hebron. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/35-29.html

**v. 29:**
- Isaac's death is told ahead of time. It actually happened after Joseph was sold (JFB). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/35-29.htm
- Ligonier says Moses places it here on purpose, so the story can move on to Joseph. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/isaacs-final-breath
- Matthew Henry sees how God changed Esau, who had once vowed to kill Jacob. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/35-29.html
- Ellicott thinks Esau is named first because he was the firstborn. https://biblehub.com/genesis/35-29.htm
- Utley lists what "gathered to his people" could mean: a peaceful death, burial in the family tomb, or reunion with loved ones after death. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-35

## 2. Differences between Protestant traditions
Most of these are different emphases rather than real disagreements:
- **Reformed (Calvin):** reads the "kings" of v. 11 as David's line only. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/35-11.html
- **Methodist (Wesley):** reads the seed and land of vv. 11–12 as pointing to Christ and heaven. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/genesis-35.html
- **Baptist (Gill):** in v. 2, unlike Barnes and Keil, doubts that the idols were Rachel's. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/35-2.html
- **Lutheran (Kretzmann):** in his notes on Genesis 49, he ties Reuben's lost birthright to this verse. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/genesis-49.html

## 3. Other views
- **Modern scholarship:**
  - The Cambridge Bible links the phrases in v. 11 to the "P" source (one of the written sources scholars think lie behind Genesis). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/35-11.htm
  - On vv. 19–20 it sees clearly, therefore, a discrepancy with Jeremiah 31:15 and 1 Samuel 10:2, which put Rachel's tomb north of Jerusalem. It suggests "that is, Bethlehem" is a later note added in error. The Pulpit Commentary and Keil reject this. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/35-19.htm
  - On v. 29, the Cambridge Bible retells the Book of Jubilees' legend that Jacob later killed Esau. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/35-29.htm
- **Catholic:** Haydock's commentary (v. 21) puts the tower of Eder near Bethlehem, where the angels announced Christ's birth. It says St. Helena built a church there in honour of the angels. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/35-21.html
- **Popular modern teaching:** at v. 16, Utley says God ensures the family's survival but not their comfort and ease. He points readers to Gordon Fee's critique of the health-and-wealth gospel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/genesis-35.html
